title.en: Rudra in every place, and the hearts of the gods

summary: Nineteen yajus, the last of the run (anuvākas 5–9) of salutations with namaḥ on one side. Most names are formed with -ya, ‘being in’, and Sāyaṇa reads them as Rudra present in every kind of place: barren land and highway, stony and habitable ground, cow-pen and house, bed and mansion, thicket and cave, pool and mist, dust, dry and green, bare ground and grass, earth and river, leaves and fallen leaves. Then come the one who threatens and strikes, afflicts a little and greatly, and in the last five yajus the kirikas, ‘the hearts of the gods’. Sāyaṇa closes by saying that each of these yajus names one form, unmoving or moving, to show that the Supreme Lord is the self of all.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa opens the anuvāka as nineteen further yajus with namaḥ on one side (विद्यमानान्येकोनाविंशतिसंख्याकानि यजूंष्याह). «इरिणमूषरं तत्र भव इरिण्यः» — iriṇa is barren, saline ground, and iriṇya the one who is there. «प्रपथो बहुभिः सेवितो मार्गः» — prapatha is a road frequented by many.

i-stem, dat. sg. pulastaye. Monier-Williams: pulasti ‘wearing the hair straight or smooth’, the counterpart of kapardin; Sāyaṇa derives it from standing before (puras) the devotees.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «कपर्दी जटाबन्धवान्» — kapardin is the one who wears his matted hair bound up; pulasti is «भक्तानां पुरतस्तिष्ठतीति», the one who stands before his devotees.

flags.note: pulasti is ‘wearing the hair smooth’ in Monier-Williams (Keith: ‘him of plain hair’), the natural pair to kapardin, ‘of braided hair’. Sāyaṇa derives it instead from standing before (puras) the devotees. The translation follows Sāyaṇa; the word table gives both. His gloss is transmitted as पुलास्तिः, with a long ā the mantra does not have.

gahvare (loc. sg. of gahvara ‘depth, thicket, cave’) + -stha ‘standing’ from sthā. The locative is kept inside the compound (aluk), and the s of -stha becomes ṣ after the e, with ṭh for th (gahvare-ṣṭha).

ca … ca, ‘both … and’: each ca follows the word it adds

sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o (P. 6.1.114)

vyakarana.note: From hrada ‘pool, lake’. Monier-Williams: hradayya ‘being in a pond or lake’. The formation in -ayya is Vedic; this edition does not decide between a suffix -ayya and -ya on a stem hradaya-.
niveṣpa + -ya. The word is rare and has no entry in Monier-Williams; its sense here rests on Sāyaṇa.

translation.literal: Homage both to the [one] in the pool and to the [one] in the mist-water.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «हृदेष्वगाधजलेषु भवो हृदय्यः» — hradayya is the one who is in pools, in waters too deep to stand in; «निवेष्पं नीहारजलं तत्र भवो निवेष्प्यः» — niveṣpa is the water of mist, and niveṣpya the one who is there.

flags.note: corrections.json (N9.7): the second witness reads निवेष्य्याय; the text keeps निवेष्प्याय, as Sāyaṇa's gloss निवेष्पं confirms (W2 error).
niveṣpya has no dictionary entry to check against; Keith renders it ‘him of the whirlpool’. The meaning given is Sāyaṇa's, ‘in the water of mist’.

The exact formation of hradayya (suffix -ayya, or -ya on hradaya-) is not settled here. Sāyaṇa's gloss is transmitted with hṛ- (हृदेषु, हृदय्यः) for the mantra's hra- (ह्रद-); the word table follows the mantra.

vyakarana.note: lopa (from lup ‘to break, cut off’) + -ya. Monier-Williams gives lopya here, after Mahīdhara, as ‘being among thickets or inaccessible places’ (Keith: ‘him of the copse’).

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: lopa is ground where grass and the like are cut off, «लोपः कठिणप्रदेशः», a hard tract, and lopya the one who is there; «उलपा बल्वजतृणादयः» — the ulapas are grasses such as balvaja, and ulapya the one who is in them.

words.meaning: to the one on the wide [earth]
words.context: Sāyaṇa: ūrvī is the earth
ca … ca, ‘both … and’: each ca follows the word it adds

words.meaning: to the one in the sūrmi
words.context: Sāyaṇa: sūrmi is a river with fine waves
ca … ca, ‘both … and’: each ca follows the word it adds

sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a vowel other than a: the visarga becomes y (P. 8.3.17), which is dropped (P. 8.3.19), leaving the hiatus

vyakarana.note: Sāyaṇa takes it from ūrvī ‘the wide one, the earth’ + -ya. Monier-Williams records ūrvya with uncertain senses (‘being in the submarine fire’, after Mahīdhara; ‘being in ponds or lakes’).

sūrmi + -ya. Sāyaṇa analyses sūrmi as su + ūrmi, ‘with fine waves’, a river; Monier-Williams takes sūrmi as ‘a pipe, a channel’ (sūrmya ‘being in tubes or channels’) and doubts the derivation from su + ūrmi.

translation.literal: Homage both to the [one] on the wide [earth] and to the [one] in the [river of] fine waves.
translation.readable: Homage to him on the wide earth, and to him in the rippling river.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «ऊर्व्यां पृथिव्यां भव ऊर्व्यः» — ūrvya is the one who is on ūrvī, the earth; «शोभना ऊर्मयो यस्यां नद्यां सेयं सूर्मिः» — a river in which the waves are fine is sūrmi, and sūrmya the one who is in it.

flags.note: Both words are uncertain in the dictionaries. ūrvya: Sāyaṇa ‘on the earth’; Monier-Williams ‘in the submarine fire’ (Mahīdhara) or ‘in ponds’; Keith ‘him in the earth’. sūrmya: Sāyaṇa ‘in the river of fine waves’ (su + ūrmi); Monier-Williams ‘in tubes or channels’; Keith ‘him in the gully’. The translation follows Sāyaṇa.

The text writes kkh, the kh doubled after the vowel of the preverb, and Sāyaṇa's gloss (आक्खिदन्, प्रक्खिदन्) spells it the same way; the padaccheda keeps the spelling of the text inside the word. flags.note: Vedic khid is ‘to draw, tear, press’: Monier-Williams gives ā-khid ‘to draw to oneself’ and pra-khid ‘to thrust away’ (Keith: ‘him who draggeth, and him who repelleth’). Sāyaṇa reads both through the causative of khid ‘to be distressed’ (khedayan, ‘afflicting’), graded by ā (a little) and pra (greatly). The translation follows Sāyaṇa; the word table gives both.

Sāyaṇa: they are the hearts of the gods, being dear to all the gods

vyakarana.note: Enclitic vaḥ for yuṣmabhyam (dat. pl.; P. 8.1.21), in apposition to kirikebhyaḥ and hṛdayebhyaḥ: ‘homage to you, the kirikas, the hearts of the gods’. As an enclitic it does not open its clause; it follows namaḥ.
Sāyaṇa derives kirika from kṝ ‘to scatter’ (kiranti); Monier-Williams gives kirika ‘sparkling, beaming’. This and the four yajus that follow have one namaḥ and no ca.
Dative plural of the neuter hṛdaya ‘heart’, in apposition to kirikebhyaḥ, with devānām ‘of the gods’ depending on it.

translation.literal: Homage to you, the scatterers [of wealth], the hearts of the gods.
translation.readable: Homage to you who scatter gifts, the hearts of the gods.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «किरन्ति भक्तेभ्यो धनानिति किरिका उदारा रुद्रावताराः» — the kirikas are those who scatter wealth to the devotees, generous forms of Rudra; they are the hearts of the gods («हृदयभूताः») because they are dear to all the gods; «तादृशेभ्यो वो युष्मभ्यं नमः» — homage to you who are such.

flags.note: kirika is ‘sparkling, beaming’ in Monier-Williams (Keith: ‘sparkling hearts of the gods’); Sāyaṇa derives it from kṝ ‘to scatter’ — those who scatter wealth. The translation follows Sāyaṇa; the word table gives both.

words.context: ‘be’ (astu) is understood: ‘homage [be] to …’

words.meaning: (formed from vi-kṣīṇa, ‘wasted away’) to the vikṣīṇakas
words.context: Sāyaṇa: the opposite of those who waste away — never subject to decay

sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o (P. 6.1.114)

vyakarana.note: vi-kṣīṇa (past participle of kṣi ‘to waste, destroy’ with vi) + the suffix -ka; dat. pl. Sāyaṇa takes vi as reversing the sense: not the wasted, but the never-wasting. Sāyaṇa supplies devānāṃ hṛdayebhyaḥ from the previous yajus to this and the next three.

translation.literal: Homage to the never-wasting [ones, the hearts of the gods].
translation.readable: Homage to those who never waste away.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «क्षीणकेभ्यो विपरीता विक्षीणिकाः» — the vikṣīṇakas are the opposite of the wasted ones, «कदाचिदपि क्षयरहिता इत्यर्थः», that is, never at any time subject to decay. With this word and the three that follow he supplies the words of the previous yajus: «देवानाँ हृदयेभ्य इत्यनुषज्जते».

flags.note: vi-kṣīṇa is ordinarily ‘wasted away, destroyed’; Sāyaṇa reads the vi as reversing it, ‘never wasting’. Monier-Williams gives vikṣīṇaka as a variant of vikṣiṇatka, ‘destroying (evil)’, after Mahīdhara (Keith: ‘the destroyed’). The translation follows Sāyaṇa. His gloss is transmitted as विक्षीणिकाः, with -ika for the mantra's -aka.

words.context: ‘be’ (astu) is understood: ‘homage [be] to …’

words.meaning: to the searching ones, the sifting ones
words.context: Sāyaṇa: those who search out and bring about what is wanted

sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o (P. 6.1.114)

vyakarana.note: vi-cinvat, present participle of ci (5th class, cinoti) with vi, ‘searching through, sifting’, + the suffix -ka; dat. pl. Monier-Williams: vicinvatka ‘sifting, discriminating’.

translation.literal: Homage to the searching [ones, the hearts of the gods].
translation.readable: Homage to those who search out what is sought.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «विचिन्वन्त्वपेक्षितमर्थं संपादयन्तीति विचिन्वत्काः» — the vicinvatkas are those who search out and accomplish the object that is wanted. Here too he supplies ‘the hearts of the gods’ from the fifteenth yajus.

words.context: ‘be’ (astu) is understood: ‘homage [be] to …’

words.meaning: (formed from ā-nir-hata, ‘struck out all around’) to the ānirhatas
words.context: Sāyaṇa: those by whom sin is struck out entirely, on every side

sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a vowel other than a: the visarga becomes y (P. 8.3.17), which is dropped (P. 8.3.19), leaving the hiatus
-aḥ becomes -o before the n of namaḥ that opens the next yajus (P. 6.1.114)

vyakarana.note: Sāyaṇa analyses ā + nir + hata (past participle of han): ā ‘all around’, nir ‘out, entirely’, hata ‘struck’, taken actively of those by whom sin is struck out. Monier-Williams instead derives ānirhata from a-nirhata, ‘of indestructible nature’.

translation.literal: Homage to the [ones by whom sin is] struck out entirely [, the hearts of the gods].
translation.readable: Homage to those who strike out all wrong.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «आसमन्तान्निःशेषेण हतं पापं यैस्त आनिर्हताः» — the ānirhatas are those by whom sin is struck out entirely, on every side. ‘The hearts of the gods’ is again supplied.

flags.note: Sāyaṇa: ā-nir-hata, ‘those by whom sin is entirely destroyed’; Monier-Williams: ānirhata from a-nirhata, ‘of indestructible nature’; Keith: ‘the unconquerable’. The translation follows Sāyaṇa.

words.context: ‘be’ (astu) is understood: ‘homage [be] to …’

words.meaning: to the āmīvatkas, those who grow large all around (Sāyaṇa); the pressing ones (Monier-Williams)
words.context: Sāyaṇa: those who on every side attain greatness of size

sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a vowel other than a: the visarga becomes y (P. 8.3.17), which is dropped (P. 8.3.19), leaving the hiatus

vyakarana.note: ā + mīvat (present participle of mīv) + the suffix -ka; dat. pl. Sāyaṇa takes mīv in the sense ‘to grow fat, become large’ (Monier-Williams: 2. mīv, ‘to grow fat or corpulent’, Dhātupāṭha); Monier-Williams gives āmīvatka ‘pushing, pressing’, from 1. mīv ‘to move’. The anuvāka closes here (॥) at the pañcāśat mark [20].

translation.literal: Homage to the [ones] growing large all around [, the hearts of the gods].
translation.readable: Homage to those who grow great on every side.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «स्थूलीभावं प्राप्नुवन्तीत्यामीवत्काः» — the āmīvatkas are those who on every side attain greatness of size; ‘the hearts of the gods’ is supplied. Closing the run of anuvākas 5 to 9, he says that in all these yajus with namaḥ on one side «परमेश्वरस्य सार्वात्म्यं प्रतिपादयितुमेकैकेन यजुषा स्थावरं जङ्गमं चैककं रूपमभिहितम्» — to show that the Supreme Lord is the self of all, each yajus names one of his forms, unmoving or moving. The division into anuvākas, he adds, matters for use outside the rite, where «एकैकाऽनुवाक एकैको मन्त्रः», each anuvāka is one mantra.

flags.note: Sāyaṇa: ‘those who grow large all around’ (from mīv ‘to grow fat’); Monier-Williams: ‘pushing, pressing’ (from mīv ‘to move’); Keith: ‘the destroyers’. The translation follows Sāyaṇa. His gloss is transmitted as मविन्ति for the expected verb form, which this edition does not restore.
